design_detail: Systematic review with meta-analyses of observational studies of cannabis use during pregnancy and maternal, fetal and neonatal outcomes up to 6 weeks after birth (protocol published in BMJ Open in 2015; no registry number given). Cannabis groups had to be free of other illicit drugs but could include tobacco smoking and alcohol use. 24 articles (19 unique studies by the authors' count: 22 cohort, 1 case-control, 1 cross-sectional; no randomized trials) were included; eight outcomes were pooled in RevMan 5.3 with fixed or random effects chosen by a heterogeneity rule: maternal anaemia, low birth weight, NICU/ICU admission and preterm birth as odds ratios; birth weight, gestational age, neonatal length and head circumference as mean differences.
can_establish: The direction and approximate size of the associations reported up to April 2014, mostly without stated adjustment, between any cannabis use during pregnancy (other illicit drugs excluded) and eight maternal and neonatal outcomes, in studies published mostly before 2000.
cannot_establish: Whether cannabis causes any of these outcomes (tobacco and alcohol co-use were neither excluded nor shown to be adjusted for, and the authors say a cannabis-only effect could not be determined); risks by frequency, amount, trimester, route or potency (not analysed); any child outcome after 6 weeks of age (excluded by design, despite the title's 'child health outcomes'); absolute risks (none reported); or whether the pooled estimates are affected by publication bias (not assessed).

sample.recruitment: Search of seven sources (PubMed/MEDLINE, Ovid/MEDLINE, CINAHL, PsycINFO, Web of Science, Sociological Abstracts, Embase; two of them are MEDLINE through different interfaces) from inception to 1 April 2014, English only, with hand-searching of the reference lists of included studies and review articles and an attempt to contact the lead author of every included study (Methods › Search strategy). The 24 included articles come from the USA (10), Canada (5, all by the Fried group, judging by the reference list), Australia (3), the Netherlands (2, both Generation R) and one each from Iran, Jamaica, Spain and Brazil (Results › Description of studies). Settings, recruitment and sample sizes of the primary studies are only in supplement 3 (not read); the total number of participants is not stated anywhere in the main text.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Eligible designs: randomized trials, case-control, cross-sectional and cohort studies (no trials were found). Participants: women who used cannabis during pregnancy and did not use other illicit drugs (for example cocaine, barbiturates, methadone), and their infants up to 6 weeks after birth; cannabis groups that also smoked tobacco or drank alcohol were admitted because few studies accounted for them. Outcomes: a pre-specified list of maternal outcomes (for example pre-eclampsia, postpartum haemorrhage, anaemia, abnormal labour, prenatal care) during pregnancy or just after delivery, and fetal or neonatal outcomes from prenatal measurement to 6 weeks postpartum (for example preterm birth, growth restriction, birth weight, low birth weight under 2500 g, gestational age, length, head circumference, Apgar and other neonatal assessments, NICU or ICU stay, neonatal mortality). English-language publications only, a restriction the authors attribute to the large number of available studies. Meta-analysis only where at least three studies measured an outcome in a consistent way (Methods › Inclusion/exclusion criteria; Abstract › Main outcomes and measures).
sample.demographics: Not reported in the main text: per-study maternal age, ethnicity and setting are in supplement 3 (not read). The authors state that many studies did not report maternal age, so an intended restriction to women aged 18 or over was dropped (Discussion, 7th paragraph); one included study was of teenage pregnancies (Quinlivan and Evans 2002, by its title). The included articles were published between 1982 and 2014; 15 of the 24 appeared before 2000 and 9 from 2002 onwards (editors' count from the reference list).
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level; attrition within the primary studies is not reported in the main text.
sample.selection_effects: English only (104 records were excluded for language at title and abstract screening, Figure 1); no trial registries or grey literature were searched; the search ended 1 April 2014, about two years before publication (1 April 2016; received 14 September 2015). The requirement that cannabis groups be free of other illicit drugs removes polydrug samples but keeps tobacco and alcohol co-use. Several included articles come from studies of drug-using or polydrug populations (by their titles: Chasnoff 1992, Ostrea 1997, Berenson 1996, Gargari 2012, Quinlivan 2002, Shankaran 2004), from which cannabis-only subgroups were presumably taken; the paper does not describe how. One positive study (Bonello 2014) used linked population hospital data on diagnosed substance-use disorders, by its title, which is a different exposure from self-reported use. Five of the 24 articles are further reports from cohorts already included (19 unique studies); the outcome-by-outcome citation lists in the Results name at most one article per cohort, so double counting is not apparent, but the studies in each pool are shown only in the forest plots (supplement 4, not read).

exposure.measurement: As defined by each primary study: any cannabis use during pregnancy, reported by the mother or measured biologically; the reviewers extracted which method each study used, but the main text does not say how many studies used each or analyse them separately. At least one included study measured exposure by meconium analysis (Lozano 2007, by its title) and one by recorded diagnoses in linked hospital data (Bonello 2014, by its title). The authors note that reliance on self-report may have led to under-reporting of use (Discussion, 7th paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not analysed. No pooled estimate distinguishes frequency, amount, timing by trimester, route or product, and the review does not discuss dose. Potency was not measured; most included articles predate 2000.
exposure.polysubstance: Other illicit drugs were excluded from cannabis groups by design. Tobacco and alcohol co-use was allowed and, by the authors' account, could not be separated, because most included studies did not exclude participants who used several substances (Strengths and limitations box, 3rd bullet; Discussion, 6th paragraph). The authors add that tobacco and heavy alcohol use are themselves established causes of low birth weight, preterm birth and small-for-gestational-age births. The review does not say whether the odds ratios it pooled were adjusted (they were taken from the papers or computed by the reviewers from reported data), and continuous outcomes were pooled from raw means and SDs, which are unadjusted; the published protocol had planned to pool the most adjusted estimate from each study.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable: exposure during pregnancy, outcomes measured in pregnancy, at delivery or in the first 6 weeks.

comparison.controls: Women who did not use cannabis during pregnancy, and their infants, within each primary study. Whether the comparison women smoked tobacco or drank alcohol is not reported.
comparison.matching: Not applicable at review level. The reviewers extracted each study's methods for managing confounding, but these are reported only in supplement 3 (not read) and were not used in the synthesis.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not shown to be controlled in any pooled estimate: tobacco smoking and alcohol use in pregnancy (named by the authors as causes of the same outcomes), maternal age, nutrition, socio-economic position, prenatal care and use of other medicines. The review's own protocol named poorer nutrition and more tobacco, alcohol and other drug use among women who use cannabis in pregnancy as reasons why earlier studies were hard to interpret.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not reported. Other illicit drugs were excluded from cannabis groups; nothing is said about tobacco, alcohol or other drug use in the comparison groups.

outcomes.instruments: Maternal: anaemia (only one included study stated the WHO threshold of haemoglobin below 11 g/dL; the reviewers assumed all used it), labour and delivery events, blood pressure, haemorrhage, hyperemesis, weight gain, hormone concentrations and others. Fetal and neonatal: birth weight (g), low birth weight (assumed WHO definition, under 2500 g), preterm birth (WHO definition, under 37 weeks), gestational age (weeks), neonatal length and head circumference (cm), NICU or ICU stay (grouped as one variable), Apgar scores at 1 and 5 minutes, the NICU Network Neurobehavioral Scale, the Brazelton Neonatal Behavioral Assessment Scale, the Prechtl assessment, and single-study measures such as fetal Doppler blood flow, lymphocyte mutation frequency and karyotype of spontaneous abortions.
outcomes.validity_norms: Quality of primary studies was rated by two authors independently with the National Collaborating Centre for Environmental Health tool for cross-sectional studies (composite score 0 to 4), the CASP cohort checklist (0 to 8) and the CASP case-control checklist (0 to 10). The main text says only that quality was high; the criteria and scores are in supplement 2 (not read), and the scores were not used in any analysis.
outcomes.operationalization: Associations as reported by each study (odds or risk ratios, mean differences, p values and percentages were extracted). For pooling: odds ratios for dichotomous outcomes, taken from the papers or computed from reported data, and mean differences from reported means and SDs for continuous outcomes, for outcomes measured consistently in at least three studies. 'Adverse outcome' was not defined beyond the individual outcomes.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. 8 counts the pooled estimates; the narrative synthesis reports on several dozen further maternal and neonatal outcomes, each from one to six studies and nearly all without an association.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable at review level. Titles, abstracts and full texts were screened by two reviewers independently, with all reviewers deciding uncertain cases; data were extracted independently by two reviewers with a third resolving differences; quality was rated by two authors independently.

analysis.effect_sizes: Exposure for every estimate: any cannabis use in pregnancy as each study defined it, in groups free of other illicit drugs but not of tobacco or alcohol; comparison: no cannabis use in pregnancy; no adjustment stated at review level. Pooled in RevMan 5.3; numbers of studies per pool from Figure 1; pooled participant numbers are not given in the main text. Maternal anaemia OR 1.36 (95% CI 1.10 to 1.69), fixed effect, 6 studies, I2 not reported. Low birth weight OR 1.77 (1.04 to 3.01), random effects, 7 studies, I2=89%. NICU or ICU admission OR 2.02 (1.27 to 3.21), random, 4 studies, I2=78%. Preterm birth OR 1.29 (0.80 to 2.08), random, 9 studies, I2=85%, not significant. Birth weight 109.42 g lower in exposed infants (38.72 to 180.12; printed as a positive pooled mean difference), random, 10 studies, I2=63%. Gestational age mean difference -0.20 weeks (-0.62 to 0.22), fixed, 5 studies, I2 not reported. Neonatal length -0.10 cm (-0.65 to 0.45), random, 6 studies, I2=59%. Head circumference -0.31 cm (-0.74 to 0.13), random, 6 studies, I2=97%. No tau-squared, prediction intervals, absolute risks, subgroup, sensitivity or publication-bias analyses. Every point estimate lies at the centre of its interval on the appropriate scale (editors' check).
analysis.covariates: None at review level. The paper does not say whether any pooled odds ratio was adjusted, and the mean differences are crude by construction (raw means and SDs).
analysis.preregistration_detail: Protocol published in BMJ Open (2015;5:e007227; received 19 November 2014, published 13 March 2015), cited by the review; no registry number is given. The protocol states that searching was ongoing and that no studies had been selected and no data extracted, while the review gives 1 April 2014 as the end of its search. Deviations from the protocol that the review does not report: the planned pooling of the most adjusted estimate from each study is not confirmed (continuous outcomes were pooled from raw means and SDs); the planned sensitivity analysis excluding studies at risk of bias is not reported; the planned meta-regression of heterogeneity was not done (the review says subgroup analysis was impossible with so few studies); reasons for exclusion, which the protocol said would be documented, are not given for full texts; and the protocol said studies would not be restricted by maternal age, whereas the review says it first tried to restrict to women aged 18 or over. The fixed- versus random-effects rule and the threshold of three studies for pooling follow the protocol.
analysis.selective_reporting: Pooling followed the protocol's threshold of three consistently measured studies, and the narrative reports null findings for many outcomes. The abstract's results report the four significant pooled estimates (anaemia, low birth weight, birth weight, NICU/ICU) and not the four null ones (preterm birth, gestational age, length, head circumference), which it lists only as outcomes analysed. I2 is not reported for the two fixed-effect pools. The planned sensitivity analysis by risk of bias is absent without comment.
analysis.power: Not addressed. Pools contain 4 to 10 studies (Figure 1), pooled numbers of participants are not reported, and I2 ranges from 59% to 97% in the six random-effects pools; the discussion states that the anaemia estimate is carried mainly by one 1990 study of 8350 women.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In studies published between 1982 and 2014, mostly cohorts and mostly before 2000, infants of women who used cannabis in pregnancy (with other illicit drugs excluded but tobacco and alcohol not) weighed on average about 109 g less at birth (38.72 to 180.12 g; 10 studies, I2=63%), had higher odds of low birth weight (OR 1.77, 1.04 to 3.01; 7 studies, I2=89%) and of NICU or ICU admission (OR 2.02, 1.27 to 3.21; 4 studies, I2=78%), and their mothers had higher odds of anaemia (OR 1.36, 1.10 to 1.69; 6 studies, one of them positive). No association was found for preterm birth, gestational age, length, head circumference, Apgar scores or the many other outcomes reported narratively. The estimates are not shown to be adjusted for anything, and the authors themselves conclude that it is unknown whether the associations reflect cannabis or the tobacco and alcohol use that accompanied it.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that cannabis use during pregnancy "may increase adverse outcomes for women and their neonates" (Abstract › Conclusions and relevance) and recommends health education on potential adverse effects. Gaps: (1) the discussion goes further, saying the meta-analysis showed that cannabis exposure in utero results in low birth weight (Discussion, 3rd paragraph), causal wording for crude associations that the same discussion says cannot be separated from tobacco and alcohol (6th paragraph); (2) anaemia is the abstract's first result, while the discussion says it rests mainly on the one positive study, which carried the most weight, and should be read with caution (2nd paragraph); (3) the Results call the included studies of high quality while the limitations say most did not exclude polysubstance use and that confounding could not be addressed, and the quality scores were never used; (4) the title promises child health outcomes, but nothing after 6 weeks of age was included; (5) the abstract omits the high heterogeneity (I2 63% to 89% for the significant pools) and gives no absolute risks; (6) NICU or ICU admission is grouped across two levels of care and can reflect hospital practice toward infants of mothers known to use drugs as well as infant illness, which the review does not discuss (editors' observation). Against this, the front-matter limitations box and the final paragraph state plainly that a cannabis-only effect could not be determined and that the effects remain generally unknown.

timeline.event: English et al. meta-analysis of maternal cannabis use and birth weight, cited in this review's introduction as the earlier synthesis. As summarized in the review's protocol (not in the review itself): frequent use, four or more times a week, was associated with 131 g lower birth weight (95% CI 52 to 209), while the pooled odds ratio for low birth weight was not significant (1.09, 0.94 to 1.27). Second-hand figures; the 1997 paper was not read.
Protocol for this review published (Gunn et al., BMJ Open 2015;5:e007227), planning pooling of the most adjusted estimates, meta-regression and a sensitivity analysis by risk of bias.

This review: 24 articles (19 studies); lower birth weight, more low birth weight and more NICU/ICU admission among exposed infants, more anaemia among exposed mothers; tobacco and alcohol co-use not separable by the authors' account.

replication.where_it_stands: The review discusses no critique, reply or quasi-experimental test of its own question. Its pooled estimates are associations not shown to be adjusted for anything (the mean differences are unadjusted by construction), from studies published mostly before 2000, with tobacco and alcohol co-use not separated, and should be cited as such. The project's list for this page holds later work on the same question (Corsi et al. 2019, Ontario cohort; Paul et al. 2021, ABCD study; Marchand et al. 2022, meta-analysis of birth outcomes), none of it read for this card; a claim about birth weight, low birth weight or NICU admission after prenatal cannabis exposure should not rest on this review alone, and must say that its estimates are not adjusted for tobacco.

funding.funder: Arizona Department of Health Services, Phoenix, Arizona, USA (as printed: financial support for this work was provided by the Arizona Department of Health Services). The role of the funder is not described.
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from the Mel and Enid Zuckerman College of Public Health (epidemiology and biostatistics; health promotion sciences), the Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology and the Arizona Health Sciences Library, University of Arizona, and one author (C Christ) from the Arizona Department of Health Services, the funder, who edited and commented on drafts. None of the review's authors appears among the named authors of the included studies in the reference list.

what_would_settle_it: Large prospective pregnancy cohorts with biologically verified, repeatedly measured cannabis exposure (frequency, trimester, product and potency) and measured tobacco and alcohol exposure, analysed so that cannabis-only, tobacco-only and combined groups are compared with adjustment for socio-economic position, nutrition and prenatal care, with sibling comparisons across pregnancies of the same mother; an individual-participant-data meta-analysis of existing cohorts reporting absolute risks would be the near-term version.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (pregnant women using cannabis without other illicit drugs, and their infants to 6 weeks), exposure, comparator (no cannabis use in pregnancy), outcomes and designs are stated (Methods › Inclusion/exclusion criteria).

A protocol with the question, search, eligibility criteria and risk-of-bias tools was published (BMJ Open 2015; submitted November 2014, stating that no data had yet been extracted) and is cited. No registry number is given; the search end date (1 April 2014) precedes the protocol's submission; and deviations are not reported or justified (no sensitivity analysis by risk of bias, no meta-regression, most-adjusted estimates not confirmed, full-text exclusion reasons not documented).
The eligible designs are listed by reference to the protocol, without an explanation for the choice; the absence of trials is self-evident for this question but not explained.

Seven sources (two of them MEDLINE through different interfaces), keywords in supplement 1, reference lists hand-searched and lead authors contacted; the English-only limit is given a reason (the volume of studies), a weak one but stated. Not met for 'yes': no trial or study registries, no grey literature, and the search ended about two years before publication.
Two reviewers screened titles, abstracts and full texts independently; uncertain cases were decided by all reviewers (Methods › Study selection).
Two reviewers extracted independently with a predesigned form; differences were resolved by discussion with a third reviewer (Methods › Data extraction).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Figure 1 gives reasons only for the 4095 title and abstract exclusions; the 860 full-text exclusions have neither a list nor reasons. Judged from the main text, which describes the content of each of the four supplements (keywords, quality criteria, study characteristics and results, forest plots) and names none as a list of excluded studies.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Provisional: the main text gives only country and design; population, setting, sample size, exposure measurement and confounder management of each study are in supplement 3, which was not read.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: The tools named (NCCEH cross-sectional tool; CASP cohort and case-control checklists) cover recruitment, exposure measurement, confounding and outcome measurement, but not selection of the reported result, and each was collapsed into a composite score; the per-study scores are in supplement 2 (not read). The main text's verdict of high quality sits poorly with the authors' own statement that most studies did not exclude polysubstance use.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Funding of primary studies is not among the data items extracted (Methods › Data extraction) and is not reported.

Continuous outcomes were pooled from raw means and SDs and odds ratios were taken or computed without any statement that adjusted estimates were used or why crude data were combined, contrary to the protocol's plan to pool the most adjusted estimates; the choice between fixed and random effects was driven by heterogeneity tests, and I2 is not reported for the two fixed-effect pools.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No analysis of how study quality affects the pooled estimates; the sensitivity analysis planned in the protocol is not reported.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The discussion states that tobacco and alcohol co-use could not be separated and that it is therefore unknown whether the associations reflect cannabis, and discusses self-report bias and inconsistent outcome definitions (Discussion, 6th and 7th paragraphs). A close call: the abstract and the 'results in low birth weight' wording do not carry the caveat, and the review's own quality ratings play no part.

I2 is reported for the random-effects pools (59% to 97%), but sources of heterogeneity were not investigated (no subgroup analysis or meta-regression, attributed to the small number of studies), and its impact on the pooled results is not discussed beyond a call for studies in more homogeneous populations.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding (Arizona Department of Health Services) and competing interests (none declared) are stated.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Provisional: item 8 can be judged only from supplement 3, which was not read; it is not a critical item and cannot change the rating. Three critical items are not met (7, no list of excluded full texts with reasons; 11, crude data pooled without justification; 15, publication bias not assessed), and three are met only in part (2, 4 and 9), so confidence in the review as a summary of the evidence is critically low under the AMSTAR 2 rules. The practical consequences: the pooled odds ratios and mean differences are associations not shown to be adjusted (the mean differences unadjusted by construction), in which the effect of tobacco and alcohol use in pregnancy cannot be separated from that of cannabis, as the authors themselves state; heterogeneity is high and unexplained; and small-study or publication effects are unassessed. The review may be cited for what the pre-2014 literature reported and for its authors' statement that a cannabis-only effect could not be determined, not as evidence that cannabis causes low birth weight, NICU admission or maternal anaemia.

key_findings.finding: Search and flow: seven sources (PubMed/MEDLINE 689 records, Ovid/MEDLINE 911, CINAHL 60, PsycINFO 17, Web of Science 1649, Sociological Abstracts 144, Embase 1506) from inception to 1 April 2014, English only, plus hand-searching and contact with lead authors; 6854 records including 1878 duplicates; 4976 screened; 4095 excluded at title and abstract (2746 not on topic, 356 duplicates, 334 animal, 235 endocannabinoid, 104 language, 290 other); 881 full texts, of which 860 were excluded without stated reasons; 3 articles added by hand-searching and author contact; 24 articles included.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Search strategy; Results › Description of studies; Figure 1 (counts read from the rendered image)
key_findings.note: The seven database counts sum to 4976 (the number screened), so the 1878 duplicates are listed as a separate line; the title and abstract exclusion reasons sum to 4065, not 4095 (editors' arithmetic).

key_findings.finding: The 24 included articles represent 19 unique studies by the authors' count: 22 cohort, 1 case-control and 1 cross-sectional study (no randomized trials); 10 from the USA, 5 from Canada, 3 from Australia, 2 from the Netherlands and 1 each from Iran, Jamaica, Spain and Brazil. The authors report that the quality assessment indicated high study quality (scores in supplement 2). Publication years run from 1982 to 2014, 15 of the 24 before 2000 (editors' count from the reference list).
key_findings.locator: Results › Description of studies; References 13, 16 to 22 and 24 to 39
key_findings.note: The abstract says 24 studies, and the design and country tallies also count 24, although only 19 studies are independent (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Maternal anaemia: reported in 6 studies, of which 1 found increased odds and 5 no association; fixed-effect pooled OR 1.36 (95% CI 1.10 to 1.69) for women who smoked cannabis in pregnancy versus women who did not, with no stated adjustment. The discussion says the one positive study (Witter and Niebyl 1990, n=8350) had the largest sample and the greatest weight, and that the result should be interpreted with caution until more studies are done.
key_findings.locator: Results › Effect of prenatal use of cannabis on maternal health outcomes; Discussion, 2nd paragraph; Figure 1 (anaemia, n=6)
key_findings.note: I2 is not reported for this fixed-effect pool, and only one study's definition of anaemia (WHO, haemoglobin below 11 g/dL) was known; the reviewers assumed the rest used it (Methods › Maternal and fetal outcomes included in meta-analyses › Dichotomous variables).

key_findings.finding: Other maternal outcomes, narrative only: precipitate labour and manual removal of the placenta were each associated with cannabis in one of two studies; no association was found for maternal diabetes, rupture of membranes, premature onset of labour, prolonged or dysfunctional labour, prenatal care, duration of labour, secondary arrest of labour, raised blood pressure, hyperemesis gravidarum, bleeding after 20 weeks, antepartum or postpartum haemorrhage, maternal weight gain, postnatal problems, days in hospital or hormone concentrations, each studied in one to three studies.
key_findings.locator: Results › Effect of prenatal use of cannabis on maternal health outcomes

key_findings.finding: Birth weight: reported as a continuous variable in 10 studies, 4 showing lower weight and 6 no association; random-effects pooled reduction of 109.42 g (95% CI 38.72 to 180.12; I2=63%) in infants exposed to cannabis in utero versus unexposed infants; pooled from reported means and SDs, so unadjusted.
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects of prenatal use of cannabis on neonatal outcomes › Weight at birth; Abstract › Results; Figure 1 (birth weight, n=10)
key_findings.note: Printed as a positive pooled mean difference (109.42 g) although it denotes lower weight among exposed infants, whereas the other continuous outcomes are printed as negative values for lower values among exposed infants; claims should state 'about 109 g lower'.

key_findings.finding: Low birth weight (under 2500 g): reported in 7 studies, 2 showing increased odds (Bonello 2014; Hayatbakhsh 2012) and 5 no association; random-effects pooled OR 1.77 (95% CI 1.04 to 3.01; I2=89%), exposed versus unexposed infants, no stated adjustment.
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects of prenatal use of cannabis on neonatal outcomes › Weight at birth; Figure 1 (low birth weight, n=7)
key_findings.note: The citation list for the seven studies includes reference 15, a UNICEF report on low-birth-weight estimates that is not an included study; the other seven references match the count.

key_findings.finding: NICU or ICU admission (the two grouped as one variable): reported in 4 studies, 3 showing increased odds (Bonello 2014; Gargari 2012; Hayatbakhsh 2012) and 1 no association (Berenson 1996); random-effects pooled OR 2.02 (95% CI 1.27 to 3.21; I2=78%), no stated adjustment.
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects of prenatal use of cannabis on neonatal outcomes › Other maternal and child health outcomes; Methods › Maternal and fetal outcomes included in meta-analyses › Dichotomous variables; Figure 1 (NICU/ICU, n=4)

key_findings.finding: Preterm birth (under 37 weeks): reported in 9 studies, 3 showing increased odds and 6 no association; random-effects pooled OR 1.29 (95% CI 0.80 to 2.08; I2=85%), not significant. Small for gestational age was assessed in 2 studies (1 positive), too few to pool; suspected intrauterine growth restriction showed no association in 1 study.
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects of prenatal use of cannabis on neonatal outcomes › Growth parameters; Figure 1 (preterm birth, n=9)
key_findings.note: The lists of positive and null studies overlap and omit one study (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Gestational age: 5 studies, 4 with no association and 1 with shorter gestation (Fried 1984); fixed-effect pooled mean difference -0.20 weeks (95% CI -0.62 to 0.22), not significant, I2 not reported.
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects of prenatal use of cannabis on neonatal outcomes › Other maternal and child health outcomes; Methods › Maternal and fetal outcomes included in meta-analyses › Continuous variables (units); Figure 1 (gestational age, n=5)

key_findings.finding: Neonatal length: reported in 9 studies (2 shorter, 1 longer, 6 no association), 6 pooled; random-effects pooled mean difference -0.10 cm (95% CI -0.65 to 0.45; I2=59%). Head circumference: reported in 10 studies (4 smaller, 6 no association), 6 pooled; random-effects pooled mean difference -0.31 cm (95% CI -0.74 to 0.13; I2=97%). Neither association is significant.
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects of prenatal use of cannabis on neonatal outcomes › Growth parameters; Figure 1 (neonatal length, n=6; head circumference, n=6)
key_findings.note: The text reports how many studies measured each outcome; how many entered each pool (6 of 9 and 6 of 10) is shown only in Figure 1, and which ones only in the forest plots (supplement 4, not read).

key_findings.finding: Neonatal assessments, narrative only: no association with Apgar scores at 1 and 5 minutes (6 studies); one study using the NICU Network Neurobehavioral Scale found few neurobehavioural changes; of two studies using the Brazelton scale, one (Fried and Makin 1987) found poorer visual habituation and more tremor, irritability and startle, the other (Hayes 1991) no difference until 30 days, then differences on two subscales; one study using the Prechtl assessment found more hand-to-mouth activity, startles and tremor.
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects of prenatal use of cannabis on neonatal outcomes › Neonatal assessments

key_findings.finding: Other neonatal and fetal outcomes, narrative only: no association for days in hospital, jaundice, resuscitation, respiratory distress syndrome, perinatal mortality, fetal distress, anomalies, abnormal fetal tests, blood transfusion, abruption, spontaneous abortion, intubation after delivery, hypoglycaemia or sepsis, nor for chromosomal abnormalities of spontaneous abortions (1 study); single studies reported more hprt mutant lymphocytes in exposed mothers and newborns and, on fetal ultrasound, a smaller inner aortic diameter, lower pulmonary peak systolic velocity and higher placental pulsatility and resistance indices.
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects of prenatal use of cannabis on neonatal outcomes › Other maternal and child health outcomes

key_findings.finding: Methods of synthesis: odds ratios with 95% CIs or SEs taken from the papers or computed from available data; continuous outcomes taken as means and SDs; fixed effect when heterogeneity was judged acceptable (Q test p above 0.10, or p at or below 0.10 with I2 at or below 50%), random effects when p was at or below 0.10 and I2 above 50%; RevMan 5.3; subgroup analysis for heterogeneity above 50% could not be done because of the small number of studies. No assessment of publication bias is described.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Assessment of heterogeneity; Methods › Data analysis

key_findings.finding: Authors' limitations: because women who use cannabis often also smoke tobacco or drink alcohol, and most studies did not exclude polysubstance use, a cannabis-only effect could not be determined, and it is unknown whether the associations found relate to cannabis or to tobacco and alcohol use, tobacco and heavy alcohol use being, the authors say, established causes of low birth weight, preterm birth and small-for-gestational-age births; few outcomes were measured or defined in a standard way; reliance on self-report may have led to under-reporting of use; maternal age was often unreported.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 6th and 7th paragraphs; Strengths and limitations of this study (box), 3rd to 5th bullets

key_findings.finding: Authors' conclusion: the effects of cannabis on maternal and fetal outcomes remain generally unknown, future studies need stricter inclusion criteria and exclusion of other illicit drug use, but there appear to be negative consequences of exposure in utero, including lower birth weight and need for NICU/ICU placement; health education for pregnant women is recommended.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 8th paragraph; Abstract › Conclusions and relevance

reporting_issues.issue: The Results state that 24 articles representing 19 unique studies were included, but the abstract says 24 studies, and the design tally (22 cohort, 1 case-control, 1 cross-sectional) and the country tally (10 USA, 5 Canada, 3 Australia, 2 Netherlands, 4 single countries) both add up to 24, counting articles as studies; the five Canadian articles are all from the Fried group.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract › Results; Results › Description of studies
reporting_issues.consequence: The number of independent studies is 19; claims should say '24 articles from 19 studies', and the design and country counts overstate the number of independent cohorts.

reporting_issues.issue: The list of 22 cohort studies cites reference 40 (Fried, Buckingham and Von Kulmiz 1983), which is not among the 24 included articles (references 13, 16 to 22 and 24 to 39) and is not cited elsewhere in the Results, and omits reference 30 (El Marroun 2010, fetal blood flow), which is included and discussed.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Description of studies; reference list
reporting_issues.consequence: Probably a citation-numbering error; the set of included studies cannot be reconstructed with certainty from the main text alone.

reporting_issues.issue: Preterm birth: the nine studies are references 16 to 22, 28 and 37, but reference 19 is listed both among the three studies with increased odds and among the six with no association, and reference 28 appears in neither list. The Methods also say preterm birth followed the WHO definition in 'seven of the eight included studies', while nine are listed.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Effects of prenatal use of cannabis on neonatal outcomes › Growth parameters; Methods › Maternal and fetal outcomes included in meta-analyses › Dichotomous variables
reporting_issues.consequence: The vote count of positive and null studies for preterm birth cannot be checked; the pooled estimate (OR 1.29, 0.80 to 2.08) is unaffected as far as the text shows.

reporting_issues.issue: The citation list for the seven low-birth-weight studies includes reference 15, a UNICEF report giving low-birth-weight estimates, which is the source of the WHO definition rather than an included study.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Effects of prenatal use of cannabis on neonatal outcomes › Weight at birth
reporting_issues.consequence: Typesetting or citation error; without reference 15 the remaining seven references match the stated count.

reporting_issues.issue: In Figure 1 the reasons for excluding records at title and abstract screening (2746, 356, 334, 235, 104 and 290) sum to 4065, not the 4095 stated; no reasons are given for the 860 full-text exclusions.
reporting_issues.consequence: Thirty exclusions are unaccounted for, and the full-text selection cannot be audited (AMSTAR 2 item 7).

reporting_issues.issue: The model-choice rule calls heterogeneity 'not significant' for the case p at or below 0.10 with I2 above 50%, although the preceding paragraph defines p at or below 0.10 as significant heterogeneity; the protocol's version of the same sentence says 'not acceptable'. I2 is not reported for the two fixed-effect pools (anaemia, gestational age).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Data analysis; Methods › Assessment of heterogeneity
reporting_issues.consequence: The rule as applied is recoverable from the numbers, but the reader cannot check that heterogeneity was low where a fixed-effect model was used; the Methods also say I2 was calculated only when the Q-test P was 0.10 or less, which would explain a missing I2 for a fixed-effect pool chosen because P was above 0.10, but which branch applied to the two fixed-effect pools is not stated.

reporting_issues.issue: The birth-weight result is printed as a positive pooled mean difference (109.42 g, CI 38.72 to 180.12) that denotes lower weight among exposed infants, while gestational age, length and head circumference are printed as negative values for lower values among exposed infants.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract › Results; Results › Effects of prenatal use of cannabis on neonatal outcomes › Weight at birth and Growth parameters
reporting_issues.consequence: The sign convention is not stated and differs between outcomes; a claim must give the direction in words (exposed infants about 109 g lighter).

reporting_issues.issue: The Results say the quality assessment indicated high study quality, without any scores in the main text, while the Discussion and the limitations box say most studies did not exclude polysubstance use and that confounding by tobacco and alcohol could not be addressed; the quality scores are not used in any analysis.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Description of studies; Discussion, 6th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The 'high quality' verdict should not be repeated in claims; the review's own limitations describe a body of evidence at serious risk of confounding.

reporting_issues.issue: In the paragraph on neonatal length, two studies are said to show a significant decrease in 'gestational length', a term used elsewhere for duration of pregnancy.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Effects of prenatal use of cannabis on neonatal outcomes › Growth parameters
reporting_issues.consequence: Ambiguous wording; from its place in the paragraph it most likely means neonatal length, and the pooled estimates are unaffected.

reporting_issues.issue: Planned methods in the published protocol that the review neither reports nor explains: pooling the most adjusted estimate from each study, a sensitivity analysis excluding studies at risk of bias, meta-regression when heterogeneity was present, documentation of reasons for exclusion, and no restriction by maternal age (the review says it first tried to restrict to women aged 18 or over).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (protocol PMC4360840), Methods and analyses › Studies, Selection of studies, Measures of treatment effect, Assessment of heterogeneity, Sensitivity analysis; review PMC HTML, Methods › Data analysis; Discussion, 7th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Unreported deviations from the protocol (AMSTAR 2 item 2); in particular, the reader cannot tell whether any pooled odds ratio was adjusted, which the protocol said they all would be.
